name: Peter II Novák
summary:
Peter II Novak was a 15th-century Bishop of Wrocław, Poland.

Born in Kravaře, Moravia (now part of the Czech Republic) around 1200, Peter II Novak rose through the ranks to become Bishop of Wrocław in 1453, playing a significant role in shaping Catholic Church policy in Poland during the Late Middle Ages. His leadership was marked by controversy and power struggles with other factions within the Church.

Novak's tenure as bishop saw several key events, including the 1454 Polish-Lithuanian union, which united the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania under a single ruler, Casimir IV Jagiellon. This union had far-reaching consequences for Eastern Europe, paving the way for future conflicts between Catholic and Orthodox Christian powers.

Despite his significant influence, Novak's legacy is complex and multifaceted. His policies have been both praised and criticized by historians, with some viewing him as a champion of religious tolerance and others condemning his actions as power-hungry and divisive.

A lasting cultural footprint of Novak's tenure can be seen in the architecture of Wrocław Cathedral, which he oversaw during his episcopacy. The cathedral's stunning Gothic design remains one of the city's most iconic landmarks today.
